name: Search Autocomplete
tagline: Grow a type-ahead box from a SQL LIKE query to a typo-tolerant, personalised index
summary: Autocomplete looks like the smallest feature on a search page and is one of the tightest latency budgets in a product: a suggestion must come back before the user's next keystroke, which means tens of milliseconds end to end, on every character, for every user. At small scale a LIKE query answers it. At scale the answer is precomputed and stored in a purpose-built index, the query path never touches the source of truth, and the whole index is derived data that can be thrown away and rebuilt. Each step keeps the previous design and adds only what the new bottleneck demands.
requirements: Suggestions update as the user types and always reflect the prefix currently in the box.
A suggestion request completes in under about 50 ms at p99, measured at the service, so the list feels attached to the keyboard.
Results are ranked by popularity and recency of real searches, not alphabetically.
Common typos, transpositions and missing accents still return the intended term.
New and trending terms appear in suggestions within minutes, not on the next daily batch.
One user typing a ten-character query must not cost ten expensive backend queries.
When a ranking or personalisation dependency degrades, the service still returns global suggestions instead of failing.

steps.title: SQL LIKE against the terms table
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. The requirement is 'show me terms starting with what I typed', and the smallest thing that satisfies it is one indexed table and one query.
steps.why: SELECT term FROM search_terms WHERE term LIKE $1 || '%' ORDER BY popularity DESC LIMIT 10 with a B-tree index on term turns the prefix match into a range scan, which PostgreSQL answers in a few milliseconds at this size. We choose it because it adds no infrastructure, the suggestion list is always consistent with the term table, and a term added by an admin is suggestable immediately. The client must debounce from day one — fire the request only after roughly 100–150 ms of keyboard silence, cancel the in-flight request when a new character arrives, and ignore responses that arrive out of order — because otherwise a ten-character query becomes ten queries and the load is a multiple of the user count rather than proportional to it. The cost we consciously accept is that this design already violates one requirement: ORDER BY popularity cannot use the prefix index, so the database sorts every matching row, and the cheapest prefixes are the most expensive queries.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Waits ~120 ms after the last keypress, aborts the previous request and drops stale responses so only the newest prefix is rendered.

nodes.label: Suggest API
nodes.why: Stateless; normalises the prefix (lowercase, trim, strip accents) and runs a single parameterised LIKE query.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Source of truth for the suggestion corpus with a B-tree index on term; the same table also receives popularity updates.

edges.label: WHERE term LIKE 'lap%' ORDER BY popularity

steps.title: In-memory prefix index with precomputed top-k
steps.problem: The database became the bottleneck for a feature that is not even the search itself. Short prefixes match hundreds of thousands of rows and the sort by popularity dominates CPU, p99 climbed past 300 ms on two-letter prefixes, and autocomplete traffic — one request per pause in typing, from every user — now outnumbers actual searches by an order of magnitude. Reads must stop doing per-request work.
steps.why: Move the answer from query time to build time. A trie keyed on characters walks the prefix in O(prefix length) with no comparison against non-matching terms, and each node stores its own precomputed top ten suggestions, so the sort disappears entirely from the read path — a lookup becomes a pointer walk plus returning a cached list, comfortably inside a 5 ms slice of the 50 ms budget. This is the point at which the index becomes explicitly derived data: it is built by a job that reads the term table and can be dropped, rebuilt or rolled back at any time without data loss, which is what makes it safe to keep denormalised and shaped for exactly one query. The costs are real and set up the next step: the whole structure lives in each process's heap, so memory is multiplied by instance count, a cold start must build or load it before the instance can serve traffic, and popularity changes are only visible after the next rebuild — a staleness window of whatever the job's cadence is.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Unchanged; the debounce is still what keeps request volume proportional to typing pauses rather than characters.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Every instance holds an identical index copy, so any instance can answer any prefix and no session affinity is needed.

nodes.label: Suggest Service
nodes.why: Normalises the prefix and walks the in-process index; returns the node's stored top-k list without touching the database.

nodes.label: In-process Prefix Index
nodes.why: Characters as edges, a ranked list of completions at each node; sized in the low gigabytes for a few million terms after prefix compression.

nodes.label: Index Builder
nodes.why: Runs on a schedule, produces an immutable index artefact and publishes it; instances load the newest artefact at boot and on a signal.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Still owns terms and popularity counters, but is now read only by the builder — never on the request path.

steps.title: Redis-cached prefixes ranked by popularity
steps.problem: The index outgrew the process. Every one of sixty instances carries the same multi-gigabyte structure, so scaling out to handle request volume means paying for memory sixty times; a rebuild takes minutes and each deploy has to re-warm the whole fleet before it can take traffic; and because instances load artefacts at different times, two users typing the same prefix get different rankings. Worst of all, a trending term cannot appear until the next full rebuild.
steps.why: Separate the precomputed answer from the process that serves it: store one Redis sorted set per normalised prefix, member = suggestion, score = popularity. A read is a single ZREVRANGE returning the top ten — one network hop of about a millisecond, so the budget still has ~45 ms of headroom, and every instance now agrees because there is one copy. Instances become stateless and cheap to add. Prefixes are capped at six characters (a few hundred million keys at most, which fits comfortably in a small cluster); longer prefixes read the six-character key and filter the result in the service, since by seven characters the candidate set is already tiny. A streaming aggregator consumes search events and applies score deltas continuously, so trending terms surface in seconds rather than at the next rebuild. The costs: write amplification, because a term's score change must be applied to every prefix key it appears in — bounded by the six-character cap and batched in pipelines; the keyspace is now durable-ish operational state that must be rebuildable, so the batch builder is kept as the recovery path and runs nightly to correct drift; and Redis becomes a hard dependency on the read path, so the service keeps a small in-process cache of the hottest prefixes to survive a brief Redis failure with degraded freshness.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Instances are now genuinely stateless, so adding capacity is instant instead of waiting on an index load.

nodes.label: Suggest Service
nodes.why: One Redis call per request plus a tiny local cache of hot prefixes as a degradation path; no rebuild, no warm-up.

nodes.label: Redis: prefix → top terms
nodes.why: Score is popularity with time decay; capped at the top ~20 members per prefix so memory grows with the keyspace, not with the corpus tail.

nodes.label: Ranking Aggregator
nodes.why: Consumes search events, aggregates counts in short windows and pipelines ZINCRBY across the affected prefix keys.

nodes.label: Nightly Rebuilder
nodes.why: Recomputes every prefix key from the term store so the derived index has a deterministic recovery path if Redis is lost or diverges.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL: terms + logs
nodes.why: Owns the term corpus and aggregated search counts; read by the builder only.

steps.title: Search engine for typo tolerance and fuzzy matching
steps.problem: Exact prefixes are the only thing the design can answer. A transposed letter ('adiads'), a missing accent, a plural, a mid-word match or a query typed in the wrong keyboard layout all return an empty list, and users read that as a broken product. Precomputing misspellings is not an option: the number of strings within edit distance two of a term is enormous, and the prefix keyspace would explode. Non-Latin scripts need normalisation the service does not do.
steps.why: Add a purpose-built index rather than more prefix keys. The suggestion corpus is indexed in Elasticsearch with edge-n-gram analysis for prefix matching, language-specific analysers for folding and stemming, and fuzzy matching bounded by Levenshtein distance one for short inputs and two for longer ones — with the fuzziness gated behind a required prefix of the first character so the query stays cheap. Popularity from step 3 becomes a ranking signal on the document, so relevance is a blend of match quality and popularity rather than either alone. Crucially Redis stays in front as a read-through cache: hot prefixes hit it and never reach the engine, so a fuzzy query costing 5–20 ms is only paid on the long tail, and the 50 ms p99 target survives. This is the clearest statement of the design's central idea — the engine's index is derived data, rebuilt by an indexer from the term store, so an analyser change means a reindex-and-swap rather than a migration, and losing the cluster costs latency and a rebuild but never content. The costs: a stateful cluster to operate and resize, relevance tuning that is never finished and needs offline evaluation against click logs, index lag of seconds behind the term store, and a fallback path — on engine timeout the service returns the exact-prefix result from Redis rather than an error.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Unchanged; the debounce now also protects a much more expensive backend query.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Unchanged.

nodes.label: Suggest Service
nodes.why: Tries Redis first; on a miss queries the engine, writes the result back under the prefix key with a short TTL, and on engine timeout degrades to exact-prefix results.

nodes.label: Redis: prefix cache
nodes.why: Absorbs the large majority of traffic so the engine sees only tail prefixes; entries expire quickly so ranking changes propagate.

nodes.label: Elasticsearch
nodes.why: Answers prefixes it never saw before, tolerates typos and folds accents per language; scores blend match quality with popularity.

nodes.label: Indexer
nodes.why: Streams terms and popularity into a new index, then flips an alias — the derived-data property is what makes an analyser change a routine operation.

nodes.label: Ranking Aggregator
nodes.why: Unchanged from step 3, but now also feeds popularity into the engine documents instead of only into prefix keys.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL: term store
nodes.why: The only place a term must exist; both the cache and the engine are rebuildable from it.

steps.title: Per-user personalisation from an event stream
steps.problem: The suggestions are fast, forgiving and identical for everybody. A user who searches one category daily still gets global top terms, their own recent queries are not offered back to them, and locale is ignored so a European user sees terms trending on another continent. There is also no stream of behaviour to compute any of this from: search and click events are aggregated into counters and then discarded, so no per-user signal exists.
steps.why: Two additions. First, every impression, keystroke session and selection becomes an event on Kafka, partitioned by user id. Kafka rather than a work queue because the same stream now feeds several independent consumers — popularity aggregation, per-user features, offline relevance evaluation, abuse detection — and must be replayable to rebuild a feature store after a bug. Consumers maintain a small per-user document in Redis: recent queries, category affinity, locale. Second, the read path gains a re-ranking stage: the suggest service fetches global candidates and the user's features in parallel, then blends a personal score into the global one and returns the top ten. Parallel fetches plus a hard per-dependency timeout are what keep this inside 50 ms — if the feature lookup misses its 10 ms slice the request proceeds with global ranking only, which is a visible-but-acceptable degradation and satisfies the availability requirement. Multi-region follows the same logic: each region runs its own suggest service, Redis and engine replicas so the network round trip stays local, while Kafka replicates events between regions and accepts that popularity converges within seconds rather than instantly. The costs are substantial: query history is sensitive personal data and needs retention limits, deletion on request and exclusion of private-mode sessions; personalisation can trap a user in their own history, so a share of unpersonalised results is always mixed in; the feature store lags reality by consumer delay; and none of this is worth shipping without an offline evaluation loop against held-out click logs, because a ranking change looks busy while quietly making suggestions worse.

nodes.label: Browser / App
nodes.why: Sends the debounced prefix and reports which suggestion was chosen, which is the label the ranking learns from.

nodes.label: Regional API Gateway
nodes.why: Autocomplete is latency-bound, so the request must be served from the closest region; the gateway also applies per-user rate limits on keystroke traffic.

nodes.label: Suggest Service
nodes.why: Fetches global candidates from the prefix cache and the engine, and the user's features, all in parallel with independent timeouts.

nodes.label: Re-ranking Stage
nodes.why: Lightweight model over cached features only — no model call may exceed its slice of the 50 ms budget, and missing features fall back to the global order.

nodes.label: Redis: prefixes (regional)
nodes.why: A regional replica of the step-3 and step-4 cache so the hot path never crosses a continent.

nodes.label: Redis: user features
nodes.why: One small document per active user, read in a single call; values lag the event stream by the consumer's processing delay.

nodes.label: Elasticsearch (regional)
nodes.why: Same index as step 4, replicated per region; only cache misses reach it.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Durable and replayable with many consumer groups, partitioned by user id so a user's events are processed in order.

nodes.label: Feature + Popularity Consumers
nodes.why: Write per-user features and global popularity; the same log is replayed to rebuild either one after a change.

nodes.label: Term Store + Click Logs
nodes.why: Keeps the authoritative term corpus and the query/click history used to evaluate ranking changes offline before they ship.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show an autocomplete service growing. Step 1: a debounced client calls one suggest API that runs a SQL LIKE query with ORDER BY popularity against PostgreSQL. Step 2: an index builder rebuilds a trie with precomputed top-k lists from the term table; suggest instances walk that in-process index and never touch the database on a request. Step 3: the precomputed answers move into Redis as one sorted set per prefix, instances become stateless, a streaming aggregator applies popularity deltas from search events, and a nightly rebuilder recreates the keyspace. Step 4: Elasticsearch is added behind the Redis cache to handle typos, accents and unseen prefixes with edge n-grams and bounded fuzzy matching, built by an indexer that swaps an alias. Step 5: behaviour events flow into Kafka; consumers maintain per-user features and global popularity in Redis, a re-ranking stage blends personal and global scores under strict per-dependency timeouts, and each region serves suggestions from local replicas.
